To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) a model of financial frictions interacting with search frictions can account for both business cycle and crisis dynamics; (b) the model can be calibrated to a Suddent Stop-prone emerging market economy as well as to the recent crisis in peripheral European economies; (c) the model predicts a large increase in unemployment during crises, and that the welfare gains from reducing real minimum wages are substantial.

1) the combination of financial and labor market imperfections can explain the large output drops and unemployment spikes that characterize financial crises in both emerging economies and in some peripheral European countries, and 2) policies that reduce real wages can mitigate unemployment spikes during crises.

(1) financial and labor market friction interact as binding constraints in a business cycle model, (2) the model accounts for the main macroeconomic features of financial crises in emerging economies, (3) the model accounts also for the unemployment dynamics of the recent Eurozone crisis, (4) the model predicts that a reduction in real minimum wages is welfare enhancing during crises.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of financial frictions and the labor market in the propagation of business cycles.
the interaction between labor and financial markets and its impact on the macroeconomy.
understanding the dynamics of unemployment and the role of financial crises during business cycles.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a reduction of the real minimum wage is welfare improving during a Sudden Stop crisis, but that this is only true for emerging economies.
the model is a useful tool to analyze the interaction of financial and labor market shocks, but that the results depend on the calibration.
the financial and labor market interactions are key to understand the unemployment dynamics during crises.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interaction of financial and labor market imperfections can account for the observed patterns of unemployment during crises.
labor market policies can be very effective during crises.
the model can account for the main stylized facts of the recent financial crises and that it is consistent with a large number of other empirical regularities.
The main takeaway from our work is that
labor market policies that reduce the minimum real wages in the presence of a binding borrowing constraint can be welfare improving.
financial frictions are important to account for unemployment dynamics in emerging economies.
the combination of financial and labor market imperfections is key for understanding the behavior of the economy during crises.
